summary: MOONFALL is an educational mission-management game in which players lead a four-person crewed mission to the Moon from start to finish: securing a budget, selecting the crew, launching, piloting the landing, running a 150-day lunar base and calling a relief ship to bring the crew home. Every decision has a physical, biological and financial consequence, computed by a deterministic simulation core written in C17 and rendered with raylib. The game answers the challenge by letting students configure a mission, manage mass, power, life support, science instruments and budget, and see why each choice succeeds or fails. Its numbers come from NASA and peer-reviewed sources, such as the 2,081 m/s Apollo descent budget, the lunar surface radiation measured by Chang’e 4, the Artemis III science priorities and NASA’s audited launch costs. Every value is labeled as verified, derived, assumed or fictional. This matters because mission design is usually taught as isolated formulas; MOONFALL lets students feel the trade-offs, learn from their mistakes through built-in explanations, and understand that staying longer on the Moon costs another rocket.
details:
What it does and how it works. MOONFALL tells the story of one crewed lunar mission in five chapters. At the Earth Base, the mission receives its budget and the player picks 4 of 11 astronauts, each with different skills. On the Ship, the rocket launches and random events (such as a trajectory deviation) pause the clock and offer three options with real costs in propellant and time. On the Moon, the player pilots the lander with real lunar gravity and variable mass. At the Moon Station, the player runs a 150-day base, splitting each day between science, rock sampling, crops, water extraction, repairs, exercise and rest, while oxygen, water and food are consumed, radiation accumulates, and muscle and bone are lost. To Return Home, the player launches a relief ship, because NASA’s Orion is designed for 21-day missions. A final report grades science, samples, safety and cost, and saves a reproducible seed.

Benefits. Failures are explained, not just punished: in-game guides show why a lander crashed or why a crew ran out of oxygen, and decision screens preview the effect of each option. Because the simulation is deterministic, a whole class can replay the same mission and compare decisions.

Intended impact. Free, offline-capable STEM learning for high-school and university students, especially in regions far from aerospace hubs (SDG 4 Quality Education, SDG 9 Innovation). Distribution costs US$0 today (web link and download).

Tools. C17 and CMake for a graphics-free simulation core with automated tests (CTest); raylib for rendering, input and cinematics; Python and spreadsheets for propulsion, life-support, radiation and science-scoring calculations. AI assistants were used for literature search and document and code review, and AI-simulated stakeholder panels gave early design feedback. Every value was verified by the team against its source.

Creativity. The story turns a real engineering limit into gameplay: staying longer on the Moon costs another rocket. Every number on screen carries a data class (verified, derived, assumed or fictional), so players learn where the data comes from.

Factors we considered. Scientific traceability (NASA technical notes, standards, audits and peer-reviewed measurements); honesty about assumptions (fictional lander parts, an Apollo-style orbit, a lander waiting 150 days on the surface); accessibility (it runs on modest computers, and it is free); safety over efficiency (if the crew is lost, the score is zero); and scalability (new visual layers can be added without rewriting the physics).
